title: A route planner
description:
Build a route planner for a network of places joined by two-way roads, each taking some whole number of minutes. It finds the fastest routes, what can be reached in a given time, the farthest place, and the cheapest network that keeps everything connected. ``` road home bakery 4 road home bridge 1 road bridge bakery 2 road bakery park 1 road bridge park 5 road park school 3 route home school reach home 4 close bakery park route home school network ``` prints ``` added road home-bakery (4 min) added road home-bridge (1 min) added road bridge-bakery (2 min) added road bakery-park (1 min) added road bridge-park (5 min) added road park-school (3 min) home -> bridge -> bakery -> park -> school (7 min, 4 roads) reach home 4: home 0, bridge 1, bakery 3, park 4 closed road bakery-park home -> bridge -> park -> school (9 min, 3 roads) network: 11 min over 4 roads, 1 part ``` Place names are single words. A place exists once a road has mentioned it, even if that road is later closed. | Command | Output | |---|---| | `road ` | Adds the road, or changes its time if `a` and `b` are already joined: `added road a-b (m min)` / `updated road a-b (m min)` (names in the order given) | | `close ` | `closed road a-b`, or `error: no road between a and b` | | `route ` | The fastest route as `a -> ... -> b (t min, r roads)` (`1 road` for one; `a (0 min, 0 roads)` when a and b are the same), or `no route from a to b`. If several routes are equally fast, choose the one with the **fewest roads**; the tests never need a further tie-break | | `reach ` | `reach a m: ` and every place reachable within `m` minutes (including `a` at 0) as ` `, sorted by time, then name, separated by `, ` | | `far ` | `farthest from a: ( min)`, the reachable place with the largest time (ties: the smallest name); `nothing is reachable from a` if no other place is | | `network` | The cheapest set of roads that keeps every connected group of places connected (a minimum spanning forest): `network: min over roads,

parts` (`1 road`, `1 part`); `network: empty` with no places | | `places` | ` places: ` (`1 place: ...`), or `no places` | **Mistakes**: an unknown place in `route`, `reach`, `far` or `close` prints `error: unknown place ''` (the first unknown one); minutes must be whole numbers from 1 to 100000 for `road` and from 0 to 100000000 for `reach` (`error: minutes must be a whole number from to `); `road a a` prints `error: a road must join two different places`; a known command with the wrong number of words prints `error: usage: ` (`road `, `close `, `route `, `reach `, `far `, `network`, `places`); anything else prints `error: unknown command ''`. Blank lines are ignored.
hints: Dijkstra works with any labels that add up and compare consistently. Here a label is `(minutes, roads)`; extending a route adds `(m, 1)`, and comparing pairs lexicographically makes equally fast routes with fewer roads win.
Number the places as they appear and keep two maps: name to number for lookups, and a vector of names for printing. Every algorithm then works on plain integers.
requirements: Give each place a number when it first appears (`std::unordered_map<std::string, int>` plus a vector of names) and store the roads as adjacency lists of `(neighbour, minutes)`.

`route`, `reach` and `far` use Dijkstra's algorithm with a `std::priority_queue`. For `route`, compare `(minutes, roads)` pairs so that ties go to fewer roads, and rebuild the route from parent links.
`network` uses Kruskal's algorithm with your own union-find.
stretch: Add `via <a> <b> <c>`: the fastest route from a to c that passes through b (two Dijkstra runs), and `avoid <place>`, which plans the next route as if that place were closed.
rules: Use Dijkstra's algorithm with a std::priority_queue.
